# Compound interest and exponential growth (`compound_interest_exponential_growth`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/math.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Mathematics & measurement (`math`)
- Deps: needs fractions_rule_of_three; helped by decimal_fractions, logarithms
- Core idea: When growth is a fixed share of what is already there, the amount is multiplied by the same factor in each period: a sum P at rate r becomes P x (1 + r)^n after n periods. Such growth doubles in equal times, roughly 72 divided by the rate in per cent (5 per cent doubles in about 14 years, 20 per cent in under 4), and always overtakes any steady addition in the end. The same law governs debts, populations with enough food, epidemics in their early phase and, in reverse, discounting a future payment to its present value.
- Pitfalls:
  - Calculating simple interest (the same amount each year) where interest is itself charged interest.
  - Trusting the rule of 72 at very high rates or over a few periods.
  - Extrapolating an exponential for ever; real growth meets limits (food, the susceptible population, the debtor's ruin).
  - Ignoring the law of the place. Compound interest was restricted under Roman law, and taking interest at all was condemned as usury in medieval Christian and Islamic law.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2400 BC – Enmetena of Lagash claims a barley debt swollen by compound interest; c. 1800 BC school tablets ask how long a loan takes to double (customary rates 20 per cent on silver, 33 1/3 per cent on barley); rome: 1st c. BC – a legal maximum of 12 per cent a year (centesima) and limits on interest upon interest (anatocismus), attested in Cicero's letters; china: c. 1st c. AD – Nine Chapters, ch. 7, problems of daily doubling and halving growth; islamic: 1256 – Ibn Khallikan records the chessboard story of doubled grains of wheat; europe: 1202 – Fibonacci, problems of compound interest; 1494 Pacioli states the rule of 72; 1558 Trenchant and 1582 Stevin print interest tables; 1683 Jakob Bernoulli studies continuous compounding; 1798 Malthus on population
- Read:
  - Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci), Liber abaci (1202, revised 1228); tr. L. E. Sigler, Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (2002)
  - Sidney Homer, A History of Interest Rates (1963)
  - Thomas Robert Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798)
